questions.prompt: Which feature indicates IRREVERSIBLE cell injury?

options.text: Nuclear changes such as pyknosis and karyolysis

questions.explanation: Nuclear shrinkage and dissolution show that the cell cannot recover. Cellular swelling (hydropic change) is the earliest, reversible change.

questions.prompt: Coagulative necrosis is the typical pattern after an infarct in the
questions.explanation: Protein denaturation preserves the tissue outline for some days. The brain, a nearest wrong choice, shows liquefactive necrosis instead.

questions.prompt: Liquefactive necrosis is characteristic of
questions.explanation: Hydrolytic enzymes digest the dead tissue into liquid. The central nervous system lacks much structural protein, so infarcts there liquefy. Myocardial infarcts show coagulative necrosis, tuberculosis shows caseous necrosis, and acute pancreatitis shows fat necrosis.

questions.prompt: Caseous necrosis, with a cheese-like appearance, is characteristic of
questions.explanation: The dead tissue appears soft and white within a granuloma. It is a hallmark of tuberculosis and some fungal infections. Appendicitis produces pus-forming inflammation, myocardial infarction gives coagulative necrosis, and foot gangrene is a dry or wet necrosis of a limb.

questions.prompt: Compared with necrosis, apoptosis is

options.text: programmed, energy-dependent and does not provoke inflammation

questions.explanation: Apoptosis is controlled by caspases and clears cells tidily in membrane-bound fragments. Necrosis leaks contents and triggers inflammation.

questions.prompt: Redness (rubor) in acute inflammation is caused mainly by

options.text: vasodilation and increased blood flow to the area

questions.explanation: Mediators such as histamine dilate arterioles, so more blood reaches the area and the tissue looks red and warm. Lymphocytes do not redden tissue, and destroying red cells would lead to anaemia, not a red appearance.

questions.prompt: The first white blood cells to arrive at a site of acute inflammation are
questions.explanation: Neutrophils dominate in the first 6 to 24 hours, and macrophages follow after one to two days. Lymphocytes and plasma cells are typical of chronic inflammation.

questions.prompt: A granuloma is best described as

options.text: a collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with giant cells

questions.explanation: Granulomas form in chronic inflammation, such as tuberculosis, when macrophages fail to clear an agent. They are not neoplasms.

questions.prompt: Which mediator causes early vasodilation and increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Histamine from mast cells acts within minutes, whereas prostaglandins and cytokines act later.

questions.prompt: An exudate differs from a transudate in that an exudate

options.text: is clear and low in protein and is caused by heart failure
has a high protein content and is caused by increased vascular permeability
is caused only by low serum albumin

questions.explanation: Inflammation makes vessels leaky, so protein and cells escape. A transudate forms through pressure or oncotic imbalance and contains little protein.

questions.prompt: Granulation tissue consists mainly of
questions.explanation: It is the red, bumpy tissue that fills a wound before it matures into scar. Mature collagen is the end product, not the granulation tissue itself.

questions.prompt: Virchow's triad of factors predisposing to thrombosis includes

options.text: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability

questions.explanation: Damage to the vessel wall, stasis or turbulence, and a hypercoagulable state together raise thrombosis risk. The other lists are risk factors but not the triad.

questions.prompt: The most common source of pulmonary emboli is
questions.explanation: Thrombi that break off from deep leg veins travel through the right heart to the lungs. Left heart emboli enter the systemic arteries instead.

questions.prompt: Pale (white) infarcts typically occur in

options.text: solid organs with end-arterial circulation, such as the heart, spleen and kidney

questions.explanation: When there is no alternative blood supply, tissue dies and stays pale. Red infarcts occur in loose tissues with dual supply, such as the lung. The lung and intestine have a dual or collateral supply, so their infarcts are red. The brain, which liquefies, is not the only pale site.

questions.prompt: Generalised oedema in nephrotic syndrome is caused mainly by

options.text: low plasma albumin reducing the oncotic pressure
raised venous pressure from heart failure

questions.explanation: Protein lost in the urine lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid moves into the tissues. Heart failure oedema is driven by hydrostatic pressure.

questions.prompt: Replacement of the squamous lining of the lower oesophagus by columnar epithelium (Barrett's oesophagus) is an example of
questions.explanation: Metaplasia is the replacement of one mature cell type by another, usually in response to chronic irritation, such as acid reflux. Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, atrophy is shrinkage and hypertrophy is an increase in cell size. None changes the type of cell.

questions.prompt: Carcinoma in situ differs from invasive carcinoma because the former

options.text: has not breached the basement membrane

questions.explanation: In situ lesions are confined to the epithelium, so there is no invasion and no metastasis. Carcinoma in situ is not benign, but it has not invaded, so it has not spread. Its cells are abnormal.

questions.prompt: The malignant tumour of bone is called
questions.explanation: Malignant tumours of connective tissue end in -sarcoma. The terms osteoma and chondroma are benign, and a carcinoma arises from epithelium.

questions.prompt: The TP53 gene, often mutated in cancer, is a
questions.explanation: p53 halts the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage. Its loss allows damaged cells to keep dividing. A proto-oncogene promotes growth and becomes an oncogene when mutated, which is the opposite behaviour to p53.

questions.prompt: Amyloid deposits in tissue are demonstrated by Congo red staining, which shows under polarised light
questions.explanation: Congo red binds the beta-pleated sheet structure of amyloid, and the stained deposits show apple-green birefringence. A blue-black reaction describes iodine with starch instead.
